turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, grab a seat. You look a bit wound up — what's been happening?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Hi, yeah, sorry. My heart keeps racing and it's really starting to scare me.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. In your own words, what does it feel like, and when do you notice it?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Like it's thumping out of my chest, really fast, and I get short of breath with it. Mostly at night when I'm lying in bed, and it kicks off before exams — I'm in my final year — or if I've got a meeting at the shop where I do shifts. It's not stress though, I'm not a stressed person, it just happens then.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. I'm hearing the nights, and the run-up to exams and meetings. How long has it been going on, and how often?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, about three months. Well, actually, it might be a bit longer, since the start of term, I can't pin the day down. Not every night — maybe four nights a week, and then those exam or meeting days on top.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): When you're short of breath, is that only with the thumping?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I can't seem to get a proper breath in. It doesn't really happen on its own.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, can I just ask — is this going to kill me? I keep googling and it's all cardiac arrest, and then I can't sleep after.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear you. In someone your age this pattern is very often not dangerous, but I'm not going to shrug it off. We'll check it properly rather than guess.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): My revision playlist is a mess, sorry, that's not relevant. I just need to know I'm not going to drop in a seminar.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're not describing that sort of story. Let's get the details straight so the tests we do are the right ones.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain when it happens?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. More a weird tightness. I wouldn't swear it's pain.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you blacked out at all, or come close?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I've never fainted. I feel awful, but I'm still there.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you drinking through the day? Coffee, energy drinks, that sort of thing.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Loads of coffee. I was going to say eight a day, well actually it's more like four or five Americanos. And Monsters, usually two if I'm revising late.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to bin the coffee completely? I genuinely won't function in the library without it.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not overnight, no. Cutting down is the aim, and I'd drop the Monsters first. They're a classic trigger for a racing heart.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or vape?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Cigarettes, no. I vape though, those disposable ones, nicotine, pretty much constantly. My flatmate hates the smell, which is a whole other row.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And alcohol?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of pints at the weekend, sometimes none. Nothing mad.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines, or bits from the chemist?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I don't even bother with paracetamol.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it bad that I don't take vitamins? Everyone on my course seems to have a fistful.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not bad at all. I wouldn't add a multivitamin for this.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies? Medicines, foods, anything that sets you off?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone in the family with heart disease, or thyroid problems?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum's got an overactive thyroid, she's on tablets for it. No heart attacks in the family, not that anyone's told me.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, I should say — last year my GP did bloods. They said my thyroid was borderline. They didn't treat it, and I never saw the actual figure.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Borderline how? Did they mention the TSH, or was that the whole of it?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): That was the whole of it. Just borderline. I nodded and left, which was a bit useless of me.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ever had an ECG, the heart tracing with the stickers?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Once, at A&E, about a year ago, the first time it happened. They said it was normal, fine. Then it vanished for ages, and it's come back these last few months.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Useful, thank you. Let me get some numbers while we talk. Pulse is 94, blood pressure 126 over 78, oxygen 98 percent. You don't feel hot.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): 94? That's high, isn't it? When it actually happens I can't even count it. Should I be in hospital right now?

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): 94 sitting here is a touch quick, not an emergency, and I can't put a figure on episodes we haven't caught. Chest and heart sound normal, by the way — regular just now, lungs clear, no wheeze.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Okay. Will I need one of those monitors stuck on me for a week? I've seen them on TikTok and they look grim.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not as a first step. I'll arrange an ECG today, before you leave — a few minutes, stickers, doesn't hurt. And thyroid bloods, TSH and free T4, so we properly follow up that borderline result.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): If the thyroid comes back high, is that my mum's thing? Tablets for life? I really don't want that.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): A high result would mean we talk about treatment. It doesn't automatically mean lifelong tablets, and I'm not starting any medicine today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the breathing? Someone at uni said breathe into a paper bag. That seems mad. And will the ECG hurt if I'm sweaty? Sorry, that's two questions.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Skip the paper bag, and no, the ECG won't hurt. Slow breathing does help that air-hunger feeling — in for a count of four, out for six. Practise it when you're calm, so it's there at night and before a meeting.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Does that actually do anything, or is it just to fob me off? I'm not anxious. I already said I'm not stressed.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's not a fob-off, and you don't have to wear an anxious label. The episodes do sit around exams and meetings, even if you don't experience that as stress. The breathing is just a tool for the sensation.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. And the vape — if I stop this week, will the racing stop? I've got a presentation on Thursday. I'm not quitting on Thursday.

[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't bank on it vanishing the week you cut down. Nicotine on top of all that caffeine is very likely egging it on, so easing the vape and ditching the Monsters is worth doing. Thursday can survive a bit less of both.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do you actually think it is? Be straight with me, please.

[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is palpitations and breathlessness driven by the coffee, the energy drinks, the vaping, and that build-up before exams and meetings. I still can't rule out a thyroid problem or an odd heart rhythm until the tests are back, so those stay possible.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): If today's ECG is normal, am I in the clear? It basically never happens in the afternoon. It's at night, which is just typical, that it hides.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): A normal tracing today is reassuring, not the whole story, because we may not catch an episode. If things are still frequent after this, we might arrange a longer monitor, but I'm not booking that now.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): I go to the gym sometimes, nothing heroic, just the bike. Is that banned now?

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): The gym's fine as long as you feel steady. If you faint, get proper chest pain, or the breathing gets markedly worse, don't sit on it — A&E, or same day with us, not the two-week slot.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks? So when do I actually come back? And are the bloods fasting, because I always get that wrong and then I'm cross with myself.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need to fast. I'll see you in two weeks with the results, whether you've had another run or not. Reception will sort the ECG and the blood form on your way out.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Okay. Sorry I fired so many questions. My bus is in about twenty minutes — is that enough to get the tracing done?
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Plenty. They'll do the ECG straight after we finish. Try the breathing tonight, ease off the Monsters, and we'll go through everything together in a fortnight.

features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
